activity_context.topic_title: Double Integrals in Plane Polar Coordinates

examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates
examples.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/86036fd86096355b969da695f812c9bf835880edd68f7991183b70a6234e3eb4.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/0cf12dd41cddb943fe8b0950cdf13a0480cfbf2620a59d8bc4e8ba8775e0e6c1.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/cf2f0a011734a56f59cce2164a82d745c84b28d1bf706531deb80bb6e0a32640.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
